content: The CSAP Special Report 13, titled Maternal Substance Use Assessment Methods Reference Manual, provides a comprehensive review of various screening and clinical assessment tools designed to evaluate maternal use of alcohol, tobacco, and other drugs. These tools range in complexity, from brief questionnaires with as few as four questions to more extensive instruments exceeding 100 questions. They can be administered either by clinicians or through self-completed paper-and-pencil formats. Healthcare workers (HCWs) may face several challenges when addressing substance use in pregnant women. These include discomfort with the interaction required to identify substance users, frustration with the additional time and effort needed for referrals, reluctance to provide interventions, and a lack of confidence in their ability to conduct screenings. Research by Gassman (2003) identified that the primary barrier to implementing screening and brief interventions among obstetricians was their self-perceived lack of competence in delivering these interventions. From a cost and feasibility perspective, integrating screening and brief interventions into routine care should require minimal additional staff time. However, there are no reliable cost estimates for these processes, as brief interventions can vary significantly in scope—from simple office-based guidance to structured behavioral interventions administered by trained counselors. Adequate staff training and resource allocation are essential, as is the availability of intensive treatment options for referral when substance use is identified. Long-term, sustainable support systems are also necessary for effective management. Brief interventions have been shown to be highly cost-effective, as demonstrated by studies such as those by Windsor (1985), Ershoff (1989), Dornelas (2006), and Parker (2007). Self-report screening methods have proven to be accurate, with Yonkers et al. (2011) finding strong agreement between self-reported substance use and urine toxicology results for cannabis and cocaine in pregnant women. Self-reporting also tends to yield higher positive reporting rates when a broader time frame is considered, suggesting it may be a more reliable indicator of substance use than toxicology screening alone. The use of validated screening tools significantly increases the detection rate of substance use. However, less than 50% of obstetricians in the USA use standardized screening instruments, and among those who do, many rely on tools like the CAGE questionnaire, which was not specifically designed for pregnant populations. Effective interventions, such as face-to-face counseling, are labor-intensive but more impactful than providing written educational materials alone. Research has shown that non-mental-health specialists can be trained to deliver brief interventions effectively in general healthcare settings. Healthcare providers should routinely inquire about alcohol and substance use in all pregnant women, starting as early as possible in pregnancy and continuing at every antenatal visit. This approach is critical, as some women may only disclose sensitive information after establishing a trusting relationship with their provider. Pregnant women should be informed about the potential health risks of substance use to themselves and their babies. Validated screening instruments are available and should be utilized, and providers must be prepared to intervene or refer patients as needed. Brief interventions, typically lasting 5–30 minutes, are structured therapies aimed at helping individuals reduce or cease substance use. These interventions are particularly suited for general practitioners and primary healthcare workers. Providers should receive appropriate training and resources to deliver these interventions effectively. The interventions should be individualized, incorporating feedback and advice on reducing or stopping substance use during pregnancy. Follow-up and potential referral to specialized treatment may be necessary for patients unable to reduce or eliminate substance use. Despite the low quality of evidence regarding the effectiveness of brief psychosocial interventions, the potential benefits—such as reducing alcohol and substance use—outweigh the minimal risks. The implementation burden is also minimal, making these interventions a strong recommendation. Further research is needed, particularly in low-income countries, to address gaps in training, screening methods, cost-effectiveness, and the integration of substance use screening with other health issues like depression.
